Aerial Wildlife 
Survey Report 
Red Deer North Saskatchewan Region Aerial Bighorn Sheep 
Survey (2018) 
 
 
Background 
Bighorn sheep surveys of winter ranges give a minimum population count and contribute to establishing and 
monitoring long term population trends. Classification of sheep populations (ram:ewe:lamb ratios) are used to 
assess population composition and recruitment. Classification of rams by horn size is completed to allow for an 
estimate of trophy sheep sustainability. Alberta’s Bighorn Sheep Management Plan’s objective for legal rams found 
during winter  surveys is 5% of the total population being comprised of legal rams following the completion of the 
preceding hunting season. Legal rams are defined as having achieved a 4/5 curl or larger. Ideally, bighorn sheep 
surveys are completed every second year and the last survey in the Red Deer North Saskatchewan (RD NS) 
Region was completed during the winter of 2015. 
All known bighorn sheep winter ranges in Wildlife Management Units (WMUs) 326, 328, 418, 420, 422, 426, 428, 
429, 430, 432, and 434 were flown during the 2018 survey. When time and conditions permit, selected winter 
ranges within Banff National Park are also flown as  part of the RDNS bighorn sheep survey. In 2018, Banff 
National Park winter ranges were also surveyed. Historically, portions of WMUs 414 and 416 were flown as part of 
the Rocky-Clearwater survey; however in 2018 these winter ranges were surveyed by the South Saskatchewan 
River Alberta Environment and Parks biologists and not reported in this survey.  
 
Survey Method 
The locations of the bighorn winter ranges are GIS referenced and mapped allowing the survey crew to survey all 
known winter ranges within the defined survey area. Ideally, bighorn sheep surveys are completed as soon as 
possible following a snowfall so that the winter ranges have complete coverage of snow to optimize sightability. As 
the winter range is approached all crew members look for sheep and tracks. When tracks are observed they are 
followed until sheep are located.  
When a herd of sheep is observed the aircraft approaches from behind and flies by with the herd on the left hand 
side of the aircraft. One of the two observers on the left hand of the aircraft completes a total count of observed 
sheep and counts lambs. The other observer on the left counts  and classifies observed rams. The difference 
between the total count and combination of lambs and rams observed will equa l the number of ewes. The observer 
on the right side of the aircraft is responsible for geo-referencing sheep locations recording counts and 
classifications.

Results 
On January 16-17, February 12, February 19 and February 21, 2018 a bighorn sheep aerial survey was conducted 
for all wintering ranges within the Red Deer North Saskatchewan Region as well as selected ranges within Banff 
National Park. Weather conditions and visibility were excellent for most days, with calm winds and complete snow 
cover on the winter ranges as well as the adjacent rocky areas. The survey was terminated on January 17, due to 
high wind conditions and deteriorating snow conditions that compromised visibility. The area which was flown on 
January 17 was flown again on February 21 under better snow and wind conditions. The  sheep observed during 
the January 17 portion of the survey are not included in the results however  the locations and classifications were 
recorded and submitted to the Fisheries and Wildlife Management Information System ( FWMIS). 
On provincial lands a total of 1,646 bighorn sheep were observed, of which 1,617 sheep were classified. Of the 
classified bighorns there were 306 rams (compared to 265 from 2015), 933 ewes and 386 lambs (compared to 918 
ewes and 344 lambs from 2015). The population ratios were: 33:100:41 (rams:ewes:lambs). 
All rams which were observed during the survey were classified by horn size. The total number of rams which were 
classified were: 70 at ¼ curl, 101 at ½ curl, 91 at 3/4 curl, 44 legal rams (4/5 curl or larger). The number of legal 
rams that were observed equated to 2.72% of the total classified sheep. In the last survey conducted in 2015 the 
percentage of legal rams observed  was 3.1% Additionally, it should be noted that 4 of the legal rams obse rved 
were in SMA 5, where there is currently no hunting seasons for sheep. For sheep populations observed on 
population lands that currently have bighorn sheep hunting seasons, the percentage of legal in the population was 
2.4%. 
A total of 419 bighorn sheep were observed and classified during the survey on land within   Banff National Park. 
Classification of Banff National Park bighorns included: 106 Rams, 224 Ewes and 89 lambs, giving a population 
composition ratio of 48:100:40 (rams:ewes:lambs). 
The total number of rams which were classified within Banff National Park included 19 at ¼ curl, 29 at ½ curl, 34 at 
3/4 curl, 24 legal rams (4/5 curl or larger). The number of legal rams observed from the total classified sheep in 
BNP equated to 5.7% of the population. In the 2015 survey,  the percentage of legal rams observed in BNP was 
10%. 
The results from the 2018 bighorn sheep aerial survey are presented by Wildlife Management Unit in Table 1. The 
results from the previous survey in 2015 are presented in Table 2 for comparison.
